findings.title: Zod safeParse result object stored as the Google credential key
findings.body:
`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the `safeParse` result (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed token. That whole object is written to `credential.key`.

The next time the service is constructed, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails because the token fields sit under `data`. Every Google Calendar credential breaks after its first token refresh, even when credential sync is disabled.

Fix: store `result.data`.

findings.title: `prisma` used without import
findings.body: `prisma.credential.update` is called, but `prisma` is never imported in this file. Every construction of `SalesforceCalendarService` hits a ReferenceError, so all Salesforce event operations fail.

findings.title: Salesforce refreshes tokens on every instantiation and still uses the stale access token
findings.body:
`getClient` now unconditionally POSTs a refresh_token grant every time the service is constructed, with no expiry check. That adds load and risks rate limits.

It also bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential sync is never used for Salesforce.

After refreshing, the `jsforce.Connection` is still built with the old `credentialKey.access_token` instead of the newly obtained token, so the refresh does nothing for the current connection.

The success check `statusText !== "OK"` is also fragile, since some runtimes and HTTP/2 return an empty statusText.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body:
When the provider response has no `refresh_token`, the function sets `data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Outlook often omits it.

In office365calendar, this value is spread over the stored credentials, overwriting the real refresh token with the placeholder. The next refresh then fails and the user must reconnect.

This runs even when credential sync is disabled, so it is a regression for all users. Missing fields should be left unset so the existing value is preserved.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys are bogus
findings.body:
`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the key "[object Object]". They collide, so the second overwrites the first.

The result is a schema with only `access_token` plus one optional junk key. Because `z.object` strips unknown keys, the expiry and every other field from the sync endpoint response are dropped.

In sync mode, expiry is lost, and Zoom computes `NaN` from `newTokens.expires_in`. Use `.passthrough()` or `.catchall()` instead.

findings.title: Sync path returns a raw fetch Response that callers don't expect
findings.body:
In sync mode the function returns a `fetch` `Response`. Several callers expect a different shape:
- Google reads `res?.data`, which is undefined, so `token.access_token` throws.
- HubSpot treats the result as a `HubspotToken` object.
- Zoho CRM and Zoho Bigin read the axios-style `.data`.

The credential-sync feature is broken for these apps. Return a normalized parsed body, or adapt each caller.

findings.title: Credential id passed as userId to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: `credentialId` is passed where `refreshOAuthTokens` expects the Cal.com user id. The sync endpoint receives the wrong `calcomUserId` and may return another user's tokens, or none.

findings.title: Wrong app slug "zoomvideo" sent to sync endpoint
findings.body: The Zoom app's slug/appId is "zoom", and the webhook keys credentials by that slug. Sending "zoomvideo" as `appSlug` means the self-hosted sync endpoint will not recognize the app consistently.

findings.title: Outgoing sync request carries no authentication
findings.body:
The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug`, with no secret header and no signature. The receiving endpoint cannot verify the caller is Cal.com.

Anyone who can reach that endpoint can request any user's fresh access tokens.

findings.title: Webhook lacks method check, constant-time compare and input error handling
findings.body:
The handler has several robustness gaps:
- The secret is compared with `!==`, which is not constant-time.
- Any HTTP method is accepted.
- `schema.parse` and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` throw on bad input, producing 500s instead of 400s.

Use `timingSafeEqual`, restrict the handler to POST, and use `safeParse` with try/catch.
